title: Complete Bed Bath
summary: Providing a full bed bath to a dependent patient, maintaining dignity, privacy, and skin integrity.
steps: Explain procedure to patient. Close door and draw curtain for privacy.
Raise bed to working height. Lower far side rail. Maintain opposite rail up for safety.
Fill basin with water 105–115°F (41–46°C). Test on wrist first.
Don gloves. Place towel over patient's chest as you wash: expose only the area being washed.
Order: face → neck → arms → hands → chest → abdomen → legs → feet → back → perineal area (last).
Face: use plain warm water. Wash inner to outer canthus of each eye with a separate clean area of cloth.
Rinse each area thoroughly — soap residue causes skin breakdown.
Pat dry — do NOT rub. Apply lotion to dry areas (back, heels, elbows) unless contraindicated.
Inspect skin during bath: redness, rash, bruising, pressure injury, edema, skin tears.
Change water when cool or soapy. Change gloves after perineal care.
Change gown and bed linens. Reposition patient in comfortable alignment.
Document: skin condition, patient tolerance, any abnormal findings.
safetyTips: Never leave a dependent patient alone with side rails down.
Test water temperature before applying — patients with neuropathy may not feel burning.
Redness over bony prominences that does not blanch = Stage 1 pressure injury. Document and implement pressure relief immediately.

title: Oral Hygiene Care (Non-Ventilated Patient)
summary: Providing comprehensive oral hygiene to maintain comfort, prevent infection, and reduce aspiration risk.
equipment: Suction toothbrush or yankauer for at-risk patients
steps: Assess oral cavity: mucous membrane moisture, ulcers, bleeding, debris, condition of teeth/dentures.
Elevate HOB to 30–45° to reduce aspiration risk.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Brush all tooth surfaces — outer, inner, chewing surfaces — for 2 minutes. Use circular motion.
Brush tongue gently to remove bacteria.
Have patient rinse and spit (if able). Use suction if patient cannot spit effectively.
Apply chlorhexidine per order (aspiration risk patients — especially head of bed <30°).
Apply lip moisturizer to prevent drying and cracking.
Clean dentures separately over basin with water. Re-insert or store in labeled container.
Perform oral care at minimum twice daily (every 8–12h) and after meals.
safetyTips: Poor oral hygiene is linked to aspiration pneumonia — especially in NPO, dysphagia, and non-ambulatory patients.
Dry oral mucosa + decreased fluid intake = increased infection and pain risk.
Use suction toothbrush for dysphagic or unconscious patients to prevent aspiration of fluids.

title: Perineal Care (Peri-Care)
summary: Cleansing the perineal and genital area to maintain hygiene, prevent infection, and promote comfort.
equipment: Warm water or no-rinse perineal cleanser
steps: Explain procedure and provide privacy. Raise bed to working height.
Don gloves. Position patient supine with knees bent and legs separated.
FEMALE: clean from front to back (urethra to rectum). Use a clean area of the cloth for each stroke. Separate labia and cleanse the urethral meatus directly.
MALE: retract foreskin (if uncircumcised). Clean from urethral meatus outward in circular motion. Replace foreskin after cleaning — leaving foreskin retracted causes paraphimosis.
Cleanse skin folds and surrounding area (inner thighs, gluteal fold).
Rinse thoroughly if soap used. Pat dry completely — moisture promotes skin breakdown and infection.
Apply moisture barrier cream to areas exposed to incontinence.
Change soiled linens and incontinence briefs.
For patients with Foley catheters: cleanse along catheter tubing from insertion site outward.
Perform peri-care after each episode of incontinence and at minimum twice daily.
safetyTips: Leaving the foreskin retracted after peri-care = paraphimosis (medical emergency). Always replace it.
Inadequate perineal care is the primary cause of CAUTI (catheter-associated urinary tract infection).
Front to back in females is non-negotiable — fecal organisms near the urethra cause UTI.

title: Eye Care (Unconscious / At-Risk Patients)
summary: Preventing corneal injury and drying in patients who cannot protect their own eyes.
equipment: Eye lubricant (artificial tears or ophthalmic gel)
Moisture chamber goggles or clear film
steps: Assess eye risk factors: GCS <8, corneal reflex absent, incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos), sedation/paralysis.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Gently clean eyelids: moisten gauze with NS and wipe from inner to outer canthus. Use a separate gauze for each eye.
Instill lubricating eye drops or gel per order (typically q2–4h).
If patient cannot fully close eyelids: apply moisture chamber (clear film or moisture goggles) to prevent evaporative corneal exposure.
Tape eyelids shut as a last resort only if moisture chambers unavailable — use soft paper tape, not adhesive tape.
Assess eyes every shift: redness, discharge, corneal haziness, foreign body sensation when patient is awake.
Report: purulent discharge (infection), corneal clouding (exposure keratopathy), or eye trauma.
safetyTips: Corneal exposure in unconscious patients leads to keratitis and permanent vision loss within hours — prevention is the intervention.
Never use dry gauze directly on the eye surface.
Consult ophthalmology if corneal haziness or discharge is noted.
keyTakeaways: Inner to outer canthus cleaning direction

title: Indwelling Urinary Catheter Daily Care (CAUTI Prevention)
summary: Daily care of an indwelling urinary catheter to prevent infection and maintain patency.
equipment: Soap and water or perineal cleanser
steps: DAILY NECESSITY REVIEW: question the need for catheter every day. Remove catheter as soon as clinically appropriate (each additional day = increased CAUTI risk).
Assess: output color, clarity, amount, odor. Report concentrated, cloudy, or foul-smelling urine.
Perform catheter care at minimum daily and after each bowel movement:
Clean insertion site and catheter tubing for 6 inches from meatus outward using soap and water — do NOT use povidone-iodine (ineffective for prevention).
Clean from meatus outward, not back-and-forth.
Secure catheter to inner thigh (female) or upper thigh/lower abdomen (male) to prevent traction on the urethra.
Keep drainage bag below bladder level at ALL times (gravity drainage). Never raise bag above the bladder.
Keep drainage bag off the floor. Empty bag when 2/3 full or every 8 hours. Use a separate container for each patient.
Maintain a closed system — never disconnect catheter from drainage bag unnecessarily.
Do NOT irrigate the catheter routinely. Irrigate only for blockage and with a provider order.
safetyTips: Raising the drainage bag above the bladder causes reflux of urine back into the bladder — direct route for CAUTI.
Each day with a catheter increases CAUTI risk by 5–7%. Advocate for daily removal review.
Do NOT break the closed system — disconnecting catheter from tubing dramatically increases infection risk.
keyTakeaways: Daily removal review is a patient safety measure
